title: WHY DID GOD CALL CERTAIN SEXUAL RELATIONSHIPS AN ABOMINATION? THE HEBREW WORD THAT STILL SHAKES THE CHURCH TODAY
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CALL CERTAIN SEXUAL RELATIONSHIPS AN ABOMINATION? THE HEBREW WORD THAT STILL SHAKES THE CHURCH TODAY

Leviticus 18:22–30 | What the ancient Hebrew actually says, why God gave this command, what Christians must understand about the law, and how Jesus Christ meets sinners with truth, mercy, and transforming grace.
There is a word in the Bible that can make an entire room go silent.
Abomination.
Some people hear it and immediately feel justified in condemning others.
Some hear it and remember the day someone used Scripture to humiliate them.
Some avoid the word altogether because they are afraid of what it might mean for someone they love.
And some quietly wonder whether there is still a place for them in the presence of God.
Maybe you have a son who recently told you something you never expected to hear.
Maybe you have a daughter who stopped attending church because she no longer felt welcome.
Maybe you are a Christian who believes the Bible but struggles to understand why God would prohibit certain sexual relationships.
Or maybe the struggle is much closer than anyone realizes.
You love Jesus. You want to obey Him. But there is a conflict inside you that you have never been brave enough to describe out loud.
And every time someone quotes Leviticus 18:22, something inside you tightens.
Before we go any further, there is something we need to understand.
We cannot faithfully defend a Scripture we have not carefully understood. And we cannot faithfully represent Jesus while treating the people He came to save as enemies.
The question is not whether we should take God's Word seriously.
We absolutely should.
The question is whether we are willing to understand what God actually said, why He said it, to whom He said it, and how that passage fits within the whole story of redemption.
Because a Bible verse pulled away from its context can become a weapon in human hands.
But Scripture rightly understood is meant to lead us toward the God who is holy, just, merciful, and true.
And the story does not end in Leviticus.
It leads us all the way to the cross.
THE WORD THAT CHANGES HOW WE READ THE PASSAGE
Listen carefully to the wording of Leviticus 18:22 in the King James Version:
"Thou shalt not lie with mankind, as with womankind: it is abomination."
The Hebrew reads:
וְאֶת־זָכָר לֹא תִשְׁכַּב מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה תּוֹעֵבָה הִוא
Ve'et-zakhar lo tishkav mishkevei ishah; to'evah hi.
A close English rendering is:
"You shall not lie with a male as the lyings of a woman; it is an abomination."
Notice something important.
The Hebrew word זָכָר (zakhar) means "male."
The verb תִשְׁכַּב (tishkav) comes from shakhav, meaning "to lie down," a verb that can refer to sexual intercourse depending on context.
The expression מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה (mishkevei ishah) literally concerns the "lyings of a woman," an idiomatic expression referring to sexual relations.
And then comes the word that has generated centuries of argument:
תּוֹעֵבָה (to'evah).
Commonly translated "abomination" or "detestable thing."
But what does it mean?
It describes something regarded as deeply objectionable or detestable within the moral and religious framework of the text.
The word appears elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible in connection with idolatry, dishonest practices, and other prohibited conduct.
For example, Proverbs 11:1 calls dishonest scales a to'evah to the LORD.
Deuteronomy 7:25–26 uses related language concerning idols and their associated objects.
This matters because the Hebrew word does not mean that a particular human being is inherently disgusting or beyond God's mercy.
Leviticus 18:22 identifies a prohibited act. It does not authorize Christians to declare that an entire class of human beings is worthless, unlovable, or beyond redemption.
That distinction is not a modern attempt to soften Scripture.
It is a necessary distinction between what the passage actually says and what people sometimes make it say.
But neither should we pretend that understanding the Hebrew automatically removes the prohibition.
It does not.
The text itself is direct.
The difficult questions concern its scope, historical setting, relationship to other biblical laws, and application to Christians today.
And to understand those questions, we have to enter the world in which these words were first spoken.
GOD WAS SPEAKING TO A PEOPLE HE HAD JUST RESCUED
Imagine Israel standing on the other side of Egypt.
For generations, they had lived under oppression.
They knew what it meant to be controlled by a powerful nation.
They knew what it meant to have their identity shaped by a culture that did not worship the LORD.
Then God delivered them.
Not because they had earned His love.
Not because they had proven themselves morally superior.
But because He remembered His covenant.
Now the rescued people had to learn how to live as God's covenant people.
And this is where Leviticus 18 becomes essential.
Before the chapter lists prohibited sexual relationships, God declares:
"After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do: and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do." — Leviticus 18:3, KJV
Then He says:
"Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD." — Leviticus 18:5, KJV
God was calling Israel to be distinct from the surrounding nations.
Their worship, family life, justice, sexuality, and treatment of others were to reflect their covenant relationship with Him.
And the chapter was not merely about one sexual act.
Read the entire passage.
Leviticus 18 addresses incestuous relationships, adultery, the offering of children to Molech, male same-sex intercourse, and sexual relations with animals.
It describes a range of practices that Israel was forbidden to adopt.
Verses 24–30 then warn that such practices defile the land and that Israel must not imitate them.
The repeated declaration is unmistakable:
"I am the LORD."
God was not presenting holiness as a popularity contest.
He was grounding Israel's conduct in His authority and covenant.
But there is another detail we must not overlook.
The passage does not provide a detailed explanation of why every prohibited act is wrong.
It gives commands, describes defilement, and places those commands within Israel's calling to holiness.
Some interpreters emphasize creation order and sexual boundaries. Others examine ancient kinship structures, ritual categories, and Israel's distinction from neighboring cultures.
Scholars also debate how these ancient prohibitions relate to modern categories of sexual orientation and committed same-sex relationships.
Those modern categories are not explicitly discussed in Leviticus 18.
We should not claim that the Hebrew text settles every contemporary question simply because we have learned to pronounce to'evah.
Knowing the original language is not permission to pretend we know more than the passage reveals.
And that is where biblical humility begins.
BUT WHY DO CHRISTIANS FOLLOW SOME OLD TESTAMENT COMMANDS AND NOT OTHERS?
This is the question many believers are afraid to ask.
And many people outside the church have been asking it for years.
"If Christians appeal to Leviticus concerning sexuality, why don't they follow all the other laws in Leviticus?"
It is a fair question.
Leviticus contains regulations concerning sacrifices, ritual purity, food, priesthood, and the life of ancient Israel.
Christians generally do not offer animal sacrifices.
They do not ordinarily observe Israel's ceremonial purity system.
They do not live under the civil institutions of ancient Israel.
So why does this passage still matter?
The answer cannot simply be, "Because it is in the Bible."
Every command in Scripture deserves serious attention, but faithful interpretation also requires understanding its covenantal setting and how the New Testament relates to it.
Christians believe Jesus Christ fulfilled the law and the prophets.
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus says:
"Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."
And the New Testament teaches that believers are not under the Mosaic covenant in the same manner as ancient Israel.
Acts 15 is especially important.
When Gentiles began turning to Christ, the early church faced a major question.
Did Gentile believers have to become observant Jews and keep the Mosaic law to belong to God's people?
The apostles did not impose the entire Mosaic law upon them.
Yet Acts 15:20 and 15:29 specifically instructed Gentile believers to abstain from sexual immorality, alongside other requirements.
The Greek word used is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term referring to illicit sexual conduct.
The precise range of behaviors included under this term must be interpreted from its context and the wider biblical witness.
Traditional Christian interpreters understand New Testament sexual ethics as maintaining the male-female marital framework while no longer requiring Israel's ceremonial and national laws.
Other Christian interpreters question whether ancient prohibitions address all forms of same-sex relationships understood today.
That disagreement is real.
And pretending it does not exist will not strengthen anyone's faith.
But neither does disagreement mean that Scripture says nothing meaningful.
It means we must read carefully, reason faithfully, and refuse to substitute slogans for serious biblical understanding.
The historic Christian understanding of marriage draws heavily from Genesis 1–2 and Jesus' teaching in Matthew 19:4–6, where He speaks of male and female becoming one flesh in marriage.
Romans 1:26–27 and 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 are also central to the discussion.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9, Paul uses the Greek terms μαλακοί (malakoi) and ἀρσενοκοῖται (arsenokoitai).
The first literally means "soft" and has different uses in ancient Greek. The second is a rare compound formed from words meaning "male" and "bed."
Many scholars see arsenokoitai as echoing the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13.
The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, uses the terms ἄρσενος (arsenos) and κοίτην (koitēn) in Leviticus 18:22.
That verbal connection is significant.
It is one reason many Christians understand Paul's teaching as continuing the sexual prohibition found in Leviticus.
However, scholars debate the precise scope of Paul's terms, especially how they should be related to ancient exploitative practices and modern consensual relationships.
A responsible Christian article should acknowledge that debate rather than disguise an interpretive conclusion as a universally uncontested translation.
For Gospel Warrior, the historic Christian sexual ethic can be taught with conviction.
But conviction does not require caricaturing those who disagree.
And it certainly does not give us permission to despise those who struggle.
Because the New Testament does something extraordinary.
After speaking about sin, Paul turns toward the transforming work of Christ.
And what he says next should make every self-righteous heart tremble.
"AND SUCH WERE SOME OF YOU."
Read 1 Corinthians 6:11 slowly.
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."
Do you see it?
Paul does not build a community around the idea that some sinners are too contaminated to approach Jesus.
He describes people whose lives have been touched by the saving grace of God.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Three words that reveal something no human condemnation can accomplish.
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not people who merely made a few harmless mistakes.
Real sinners.
People with painful histories.
People who have wounded others.
People carrying secret shame.
People who have built their identity around desires, achievements, relationships, or habits that cannot save them.
People who desperately need mercy.
And here is something the church must never forget.
The passage does not give us permission to single out one group while excusing everyone else.
Paul's surrounding list includes multiple kinds of wrongdoing.
Sexual immorality.
Adultery.
Greed.
Theft.
Drunkenness.
Verbal abuse.
Fraud.
And then he says:
"And such were some of you."
The ground beneath the cross is level.
Not because every sin is identical in its consequences.
Not because every person's story is the same.
But because no sinner can earn salvation through personal righteousness.
Every one of us needs grace.
The married man secretly watching pornography cannot use Leviticus to make himself morally superior to his unmarried neighbor.
The church leader committing adultery cannot preach holiness while hiding his betrayal.
The Christian who humiliates someone struggling with sexuality cannot pretend cruelty becomes righteous simply because it is wrapped in biblical vocabulary.
And the person who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy must not be told that the hypocrisy represents the heart of Jesus.
God's holiness exposes all of us. God's grace invites all of us to come to Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Not selective outrage.
Not spiritual superiority.
Not permission to continue knowingly in sin.
But repentance and faith in the Savior who died and rose again.
THE DANGER OF CALLING PEOPLE WHAT GOD CALLED AN ACT
Imagine someone walking into church for the first time in years.
They have rehearsed the decision all morning.
They almost turned around in the parking lot.
They have heard enough angry sermons online to expect rejection.
But something inside them still longs for God.
They sit near the back.
They listen.
And then someone speaks about abomination.
Not with careful explanation.
Not with tears.
Not with the humility of a fellow sinner.
But with visible disgust.
The person hears a message that sounds like this:
"You are the kind of person God cannot stand."
And before anyone has the opportunity to speak with them, they leave.
Now consider the tragedy.
The Bible teaches that every human being is made in the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 establishes human dignity in creation.
That dignity does not disappear because of someone's desires, history, beliefs, or moral failures.
We can believe that a particular action violates God's will without denying the humanity of the person involved.
We can maintain biblical convictions without mockery.
We can call people to repentance without humiliation.
And we can welcome someone into a church community without pretending that every theological disagreement has disappeared.
Jesus Himself was described as receiving sinners and eating with them.
In Luke 5:31–32, He explains that He came to call sinners to repentance.
Notice both truths.
He welcomed sinners.
And He called sinners to repentance.
Neither truth cancels the other.
A church that refuses to welcome people has forgotten the mercy of Christ.
A church that refuses to speak about repentance has forgotten the message of Christ.
But a church that speaks about repentance without love has also forgotten something essential.
Jesus did not tell His disciples to make people feel worthless.
He commanded them to love one another.
And He warned against hypocritical judgment.
Before you confront someone else's life, ask whether you have brought your own life honestly before God.
Because the Word of God is not a stone we throw from a safe distance.
It is a light under which we must first stand ourselves.
WHAT IF THE PERSON STRUGGLING IS SOMEONE YOU LOVE?
This is where the conversation stops being theoretical.
A mother sits at the kitchen table.
Her son has just shared something deeply personal.
His hands are shaking.
He has spent years wondering whether telling the truth will cost him his family.
His mother believes Scripture.
She also loves her son more deeply than words can express.
Now she faces a moment she never prepared for.
What should she say?
Perhaps the most important first words are not an argument.
Perhaps they are:
"I love you. Thank you for trusting me enough to tell me."
That is not a denial of biblical conviction.
It is an acknowledgment of a relationship that should not be destroyed by panic.
A parent can listen without immediately resolving every theological question.
A pastor can show compassion without abandoning his beliefs.
A Christian friend can disagree respectfully without turning someone's vulnerability into public gossip.
And a person experiencing same-sex attraction should not be automatically accused of choosing every feeling they experience.
Within traditional Christian theology, a distinction is often made between experiencing an attraction and deliberately acting upon it.
Christians also differ in how they understand temptation, desire, and moral responsibility.
But whatever one's theological position, no one should be pressured into shame, coercion, or the belief that God's love must be purchased through pretending.
The Christian call to discipleship is demanding for everyone.
Jesus calls all His followers to deny themselves and follow Him.
For some, obedience involves resisting sexual temptation.
For others, it involves ending an adulterous relationship.
For others, it means confronting pornography, greed, pride, dishonesty, or bitterness.
For all of us, it means learning to surrender our lives to Christ.
And surrender is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it is a quiet prayer spoken through tears.
"Lord, I do not understand everything. But I want to know You. Teach me to walk in truth."
God is not intimidated by an honest prayer.
HOLINESS WITHOUT LOVE BECOMES CRUELTY. LOVE WITHOUT TRUTH BECOMES SENTIMENTALITY. BUT IN JESUS CHRIST, GRACE AND TRUTH MEET.
John 1:14 describes Jesus as full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And that is what makes Christ different from the religious performances we sometimes mistake for Christianity.
He does not need us to dilute His teaching.
He does not need us to exaggerate His teaching.
He calls us to follow Him faithfully.
That means refusing to make a single sexual issue the entire definition of Christianity.
It also means refusing to act as though sexual ethics are irrelevant to Christian discipleship.
Our bodies matter.
Our relationships matter.
Our choices matter.
And our treatment of other people matters.
In fact, Jesus identified love for God and love for neighbor as the greatest commandments.
That means the Christian who speaks accurately about sexual morality but treats others with contempt has not fulfilled the whole calling of Christ.
And the Christian who wants to love others must still wrestle honestly with what God has revealed.
This is not an easy tension.
It was never meant to be solved by cruelty or denial.
It calls for biblical conviction, patient teaching, humility, repentance, and love.
And sometimes, it requires the courage to admit that we have spoken with more certainty than our understanding justified.
THE CROSS IS WHERE EVERY ONE OF US LOSES THE RIGHT TO BOAST
Now picture Calvary.
Not as a decorative cross hanging on a church wall.
But as the place where the Son of God suffered for sinners.
The crowd mocks Him.
The soldiers divide His garments.
His disciples have scattered.
And Jesus is crucified.
The One who had no sin bears the suffering of the cross.
This is where the Christian message reaches its center.
Not in the ability to identify someone else's failures.
Not in winning an argument about a Hebrew word.
Not in proving that our moral record is cleaner than our neighbor's.
But in Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had fixed ourselves.
Not after we had resolved every internal struggle.
Not after we had learned enough theology to impress anyone.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word.
The Gospel is not a promise that following Jesus will remove every difficult feeling or settle every painful question immediately.
It is the good news that forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life are found in Jesus Christ.
Repentance matters.
Faith matters.
Obedience matters.
But none of these gives us grounds to boast over another human being.
Our salvation rests on Christ.
And if we truly believe that, our conversations about sexuality should sound different from the cruelty of the world.
There should be conviction.
There should be compassion.
There should be courage.
There should be patience.
And there should always be room for someone to hear the invitation of Jesus.
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." — Matthew 11:28, KJV
SO WHY DID LEVITICUS CALL IT AN ABOMINATION?
Because within the covenant law given to Israel, the sexual act described in Leviticus 18:22 was prohibited and classified as to'evah—something detestable under that law.
The surrounding chapter places the prohibition among practices Israel was commanded to avoid as part of its distinct covenant life.
The passage is concerned with conduct, holiness, defilement, and obedience to the LORD.
It does not explicitly discuss modern sexual orientation as a psychological category.
It does not provide a comprehensive account of every modern relationship.
And it does not authorize hatred, harassment, or dehumanization.
Historic Christian interpretation generally understands the prohibition as consistent with the Bible's wider sexual ethic, including the New Testament's teaching on sexual morality.
Other Christian interpreters disagree about its application to contemporary same-sex relationships.
The disagreement deserves serious engagement with Scripture, language, history, and theology.
But one truth must remain nonnegotiable for Christians on every side of the discussion:
No one is saved by being heterosexual. No one is saved by being married. No one is saved by winning a theological argument. Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And no one has earned the right to mistreat another person in His name.
That should humble every one of us.
Especially those of us who preach.
Especially those of us who teach.
Especially those of us who have used biblical truth more eagerly to expose someone else's sin than to confess our own.
Maybe the most uncomfortable question raised by this passage is not simply, "Why did God call this act an abomination?"
Maybe it is also:
"Have I allowed my confidence about someone else's sin to blind me to the sins in my own heart?"
Because it is possible to defend a biblical command while violating the biblical command to love your neighbor.
And it is possible to speak about holiness while refusing to practice humility.
If this article has exposed pride, hidden compromise, fear, or a wound you have been carrying, do not run from God.
Come to Him.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him for it.
If you need wisdom, seek it.
If you have mistreated someone, make it right.
If you are struggling with questions about your sexuality and your faith, do not assume that you must face them alone.
Seek mature, compassionate Christians who will listen carefully, handle Scripture responsibly, respect your dignity, and walk with you patiently.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony for anyone.
You do not have to pretend the struggle is easy.
And you do not have to abandon honest questions to begin seeking Jesus.
BEFORE YOU CLOSE THIS ARTICLE, THERE IS ONE MORE PERSON I WANT YOU TO THINK ABOUT.
Someone you know is silently struggling.
Perhaps they are ashamed of their past.
Perhaps they have been wounded by a church.
Perhaps they have been using the Bible to condemn everyone except themselves.
Perhaps they believe Jesus would never welcome them.
They might never tell you.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create an audience addicted to outrage.
Not to turn people's pain into religious entertainment.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
Add a few words about what challenged you.
Not because sharing makes you more righteous.
But because someone in your circle may need to encounter a more faithful and compassionate explanation of God's Word.
But I also want to ask you something more personal.
What did this passage confront in your own heart?
Was it pride?
Was it fear?
Was it the way you have treated someone who struggles differently from you?
Was it your own need for repentance?
Or was it the realization that you have been afraid to approach Jesus because of something in your life?
You do not have to disclose private details or expose another person's story.
The goal is not public confession for its own sake.
The goal is to help one another turn toward Jesus.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical encouragement, Christian teaching, and discipleship resources accessible to people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
These resources are part of a mission worth sustaining and expanding.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, not coerced.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
You do not have to give money to earn His favor.
And your spiritual standing before Jesus is not determined by a monthly payment.
But if this ministry has helped you, and you have the means and desire to help it serve others, your partnership can be a meaningful act of generosity.
These are simply gifts of appreciation for those helping sustain the work.
The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is making biblical truth more accessible.
It is encouraging weary believers.
It is helping families encounter Scripture.
It is reminding people that their story does not have to end where their deepest shame began.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep asking difficult questions.
Keep showing mercy.
Keep refusing to turn people into enemies.
Keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because when the world hears the word abomination, it may expect another argument filled with anger.
But when people encounter Christians shaped by the crucified and risen Christ, they should also encounter humility, compassion, holiness, and hope.
The law reveals the seriousness of sin.
The Gospel reveals the greatness of the Savior.
And grace does not mean sin was never serious.
It means God's mercy is greater than any sinner's ability to save themselves.
The person you were ready to condemn may be the very person Jesus is calling you to love—and the heart He wants to confront first may be your own.
